questions.question: In Oracle Automatic Storage Management (ASM), which striping configuration and Allocation Unit (AU) subdivision pattern is assigned to Online Redo Logs (ORLs), Control Files, and Flashback Logs?

answerOptions.text: Fine-grained striping with 128 KB stripe sets optimized for low-latency write operations
answerOptions.rationale: Fine-grained striping breaks Allocation Units into 128 KB stripe sets to distribute rapid, small-payload concurrent write operations across physical devices.

answerOptions.text: Coarse-grained striping with full 1 MB to 4 MB Allocation Units optimized for large sequential reads
answerOptions.rationale: Coarse-grained striping uses full Allocation Units of 1 MB or larger and is intended for sequential files like data files and RMAN backups.

answerOptions.text: Fine-grained striping with 1 MB Allocation Units optimized for parallel database table scans
answerOptions.rationale: Fine-grained striping subdivides Allocation Units into 128 KB chunks rather than whole 1 MB blocks.

answerOptions.text: Coarse-grained striping with 128 KB Allocation Units optimized for RMAN backup sets
answerOptions.rationale: Coarse-grained striping uses full Allocation Units rather than 128 KB subdivisions, and RMAN backups use coarse-grained striping.

questions.hint: Consider which striping strategy subdivides Allocation Units into smaller 128 KB chunks to handle rapid, small write operations.

questions.question: Which failure group configuration and mirroring strategy defines High Redundancy in Oracle ASM?

answerOptions.text: 3-way mirroring requiring a minimum of three Failure Groups
answerOptions.rationale: High Redundancy enforces 3-way mirroring across at least three Failure Groups, making it standard for mission-critical IFS setups.

answerOptions.text: 2-way mirroring requiring a minimum of two Failure Groups
answerOptions.rationale: Two-way mirroring across a minimum of two Failure Groups defines Normal Redundancy rather than High Redundancy.

answerOptions.text: Delegated hardware-level RAID 10 mirroring with zero Failure Groups
answerOptions.rationale: Delegating protection entirely to underlying enterprise SAN controllers without ASM mirroring represents External Redundancy.

answerOptions.text: 4-way mirroring requiring a minimum of two Failure Groups
answerOptions.rationale: ASM High Redundancy specifies 3-way mirroring and requires at least three distinct Failure Groups.

questions.hint: Think about the number of data copies created in mission-critical environments needing protection against multiple failures.

questions.question: According to ASM disk group architecture guidelines for IFS Applications, which files should be placed in the RECO disk group to isolate recovery operations from core transactional disk I/O?

answerOptions.text: Archive logs, RMAN backup sets, control file copies, Flashback logs, and multiplexed copies of online redo logs
answerOptions.rationale: The RECO (or FRA) disk group is dedicated to recovery assets to prevent archive and backup processes from competing for primary transactional bandwidth.

answerOptions.text: Active data files, index tablespaces, system tablespaces (SYSTEM, SYSAUX), and temporary files
answerOptions.rationale: Primary database assets supporting active online processing belong in the DATA disk group.

answerOptions.text: Primary online redo log groups, active index tablespaces, and user tablespace data files
answerOptions.rationale: Active tablespaces and primary online redo logs reside in DATA to maintain high transactional throughput.

answerOptions.text: System tablespaces, temporary files, and primary operational data files only
answerOptions.rationale: System and temporary data files are active operational assets assigned to the DATA disk group.

questions.hint: Focus on storage files specifically used for backup, historical recovery, and archive tracking.

questions.question: What is the primary operational objective of implementing Hash Partitioning on high-concurrency staging or interface tables in an IFS database?

answerOptions.text: To distribute data evenly across a specified number of partitions and prevent I/O hotspots
answerOptions.rationale: Hash partitioning applies a hashing algorithm on key columns to spread writes uniformly, eliminating physical disk bottlenecks on write-heavy tables.

answerOptions.text: To group rows into partitions based on discrete ranges of transaction timestamps
answerOptions.rationale: Mapping rows by date ranges describes Range Partitioning rather than Hash Partitioning.

answerOptions.text: To organize rows explicitly by categorical business units or regional site codes
answerOptions.rationale: Assigning data by specific discrete key values represents List Partitioning.

answerOptions.text: To allow instant removal of historical partitions without performing SQL DELETE operations
answerOptions.rationale: Instant dropping of old chronological data partitions is an operational benefit of Range Partitioning.

questions.hint: Recall which partitioning algorithm spreads incoming rows uniformly to avoid single-disk bottlenecks.

questions.question: How do Local Indexes behave during Partition Maintenance Operations (PMO), such as dropping or splitting a table partition?

answerOptions.text: They update automatically in alignment with table partitions without rebuilding the entire index tree
answerOptions.rationale: Local indexes share the partitioning schema of the target table, allowing individual index partition maintenance without invalidating the rest of the index tree.

answerOptions.text: They become UNUSABLE across all partitions and require a mandatory full index rebuild
answerOptions.rationale: Global indexes, rather than local indexes, typically require rebuilding or maintenance after specific partition operations.

answerOptions.text: They span all table partitions independently and lock the entire table during maintenance
answerOptions.rationale: Local indexes do not span across all partitions independently; each index partition corresponds to exactly one table partition.

answerOptions.text: They require manual conversion into global indexes prior to executing any maintenance command
answerOptions.rationale: Local indexes maintain their partitioned alignment automatically during maintenance commands.

questions.hint: Consider how index structure alignment with underlying partitions affects maintenance overhead.

questions.question: In Oracle Enterprise Manager (OEM) metric threshold management, what standard utilization percentages are recommended for Warning and Critical alerts on storage targets?

answerOptions.text: 85% capacity for Warning Thresholds and 95% capacity for Critical Thresholds
answerOptions.rationale: Setting warning alerts at 85% and critical alerts at 95% enables proactive capacity expansion before complete storage exhaustion occurs.

answerOptions.text: 75% capacity for Warning Thresholds and 90% capacity for Critical Thresholds
answerOptions.rationale: Standard storage administration baselines in OEM utilize 85% for early warning and 95% for urgent intervention.

answerOptions.text: 80% capacity for Warning Thresholds and 100% capacity for Critical Thresholds
answerOptions.rationale: Critical thresholds are established at 95% so DBAs can act before reaching 100% capacity and suffering database halts.

answerOptions.text: 90% capacity for Warning Thresholds and 99% capacity for Critical Thresholds
answerOptions.rationale: A 90% warning threshold leaves inadequate time for planned maintenance compared to the standard 85% threshold.

questions.hint: Identify the standard two percentage boundaries that provide early maintenance notice and urgent outage prevention.

questions.question: Which PL/SQL procedure and metric constant are used to programmatically register tablespace warning and critical alert boundaries in Oracle Database?

answerOptions.text: DBMS_SERVER_ALERT.SET_THRESHOLD with DBMS_SERVER_ALERT.TABLESPACE_SPACE_USAGE
answerOptions.rationale: Executing DBMS_SERVER_ALERT.SET_THRESHOLD with the TABLESPACE_SPACE_USAGE metric constant configures automated alerts for logical tablespace capacity.

answerOptions.text: DBMS_STORAGE_MGMT.SET_ALERT with DBMS_STORAGE_MGMT.TABLESPACE_USAGE
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Database utilizes the DBMS_SERVER_ALERT package rather than a non-existent DBMS_STORAGE_MGMT package.

answerOptions.text: DBMS_ASM_ALERT.MODIFY_THRESHOLD with DBMS_ASM_ALERT.DISK_FREE_SPACE
answerOptions.rationale: Logical tablespace thresholds inside the database engine are maintained via DBMS_SERVER_ALERT.

answerOptions.text: DBMS_MONITOR.SET_ALERT_THRESHOLD with DBMS_MONITOR.SPACE_LIMIT
answerOptions.rationale: The DBMS_MONITOR package is used for application tracing and statistics gathering, not for setting tablespace alerts.

questions.hint: Look for the server alert package that manages database threshold parameters.

questions.question: Which dynamic performance view can a DBA query when connected to an ASM instance (+ASM) to inspect total MB, free MB, and redundancy models across disk groups?

answerOptions.text: V$ASM_DISKGROUP
answerOptions.rationale: Querying V$ASM_DISKGROUP returns capacity metrics, free space, Allocation Unit sizes, and redundancy settings for all mounted ASM disk groups.

answerOptions.text: V$ASM_ALIAS
answerOptions.rationale: V$ASM_ALIAS maps user-defined file names and aliases to internal ASM file numbers.

answerOptions.text: V$ASM_FILE
answerOptions.rationale: V$ASM_FILE details individual file striping, space consumption, and file types rather than aggregate disk group totals.

answerOptions.text: DBA_THRESHOLDS
answerOptions.rationale: DBA_THRESHOLDS displays alert threshold parameters registered in the database, not physical ASM storage metrics.

questions.hint: Select the view whose name directly references aggregate ASM disk group metrics.

questions.question: According to technical documentation for IFS Cloud (Release 25R1), what structural limitation applies when deploying Oracle Database Standard Edition 2?

answerOptions.text: It is limited to 1 CDB, 3 PDBs, and 16 threads
answerOptions.rationale: IFS Cloud documentation specifies that Standard Edition 2 deployment is limited to 1 Container Database, up to 3 Pluggable Databases, and a maximum of 16 threads.

answerOptions.text: It is limited to 1 CDB, 1 PDB, and 8 threads
answerOptions.rationale: Standard Edition 2 support guidelines permit up to 3 PDBs and 16 threads.

answerOptions.text: It is restricted strictly to non-production development environments
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Database Express Edition (XE), not Standard Edition 2, is documented as restricted strictly to development usage.

answerOptions.text: It requires an extra license for Oracle RAC One Node in all environments
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle RAC One Node is included with Standard Edition 2, whereas it incurs an extra cost in Enterprise Edition.

questions.hint: Recall the exact constraints listed for Standard Edition 2 regarding CDB count, PDB count, and processing threads.

questions.question: According to technical documentation for IFS Applications 10, what constraint governs the Multitenant architecture deployment?

answerOptions.text: Only one pluggable database per container is supported
answerOptions.rationale: IFS Applications 10 documentation explicitly notes that although Oracle Multitenant is supported, only single-PDB container setups are verified.

answerOptions.text: Up to three pluggable databases per container are supported
answerOptions.rationale: While Oracle SE2 allows 3 PDBs generally, IFS Applications 10 support specifically limits deployment to one PDB per CDB.

answerOptions.text: Up to sixteen pluggable databases per container are supported
answerOptions.rationale: Multiple PDBs per container are not supported for IFS Applications 10.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Multitenant is not supported or verified for IFS Applications 10
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Multitenant is supported and verified for IFS Applications 10 under the single-PDB restriction.

questions.hint: Check the specific container-to-pluggable database ratio stated in the IFS Applications 10 compatibility matrix.

questions.question: Which Oracle Management Pack is documented as required for generating Automatic Workload Repository (AWR) and Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM) reports?

answerOptions.text: Oracle Diagnostics Pack
answerOptions.rationale: IFS documentation states that Oracle Diagnostics Pack is verified on IFS Applications 9 and 10 and is required for AWR and ADDM.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Tuning Pack
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Tuning Pack requires Diagnostics Pack and provides SQL Tuning Advisor and Access Advisor, but AWR/ADDM fundamental data collection depends on Diagnostics Pack.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Cloud Management Pack for Oracle Database
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Cloud Management Pack is marked as not tested or verified for IFS Cloud.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Database Lifecycle Management Pack
answerOptions.rationale: Database Lifecycle Management Pack is not tested or verified for IFS Cloud and does not generate AWR or ADDM.

questions.hint: Identify the management pack responsible for core performance data collection and diagnostic reports.

questions.question: According to IFS Cloud documentation, which Oracle Database option is required to enable In-Memory column store functionality in IFS Applications 10?

answerOptions.text: Oracle Database In-Memory
answerOptions.rationale: The documentation specifies that utilizing In-Memory capabilities in IFS Applications 10 explicitly requires the Oracle Database In-Memory option.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Advanced Compression
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle Advanced Compression provides features like Advanced Row and LOB compression, not the In-Memory column store.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Real Application Clusters (Oracle RAC)
answerOptions.rationale: Oracle RAC provides multi-node database clustering rather than column-store memory acceleration.

answerOptions.text: Oracle Active Data Guard
answerOptions.rationale: Active Data Guard provides read-only standby database replication, not in-memory processing.

questions.hint: Look for the specific option named after the feature required for column-store memory execution.
